clips.text: Look around the pond. Sort the living and nonliving things. Find what a plant needs.
Choose a group for each card.
Which set supplies a green plant with water, light, and air? A. Water + sunlight + air B. Rocks + toys + sand C. A dark, dry box
Water, light, and air help green plants meet their needs. Plants also need suitable conditions and minerals.
Living things get what they need from their environment.
environment
Follow the water through the plant. Match each part to its job.
Tap the water pathway in order. Then match two animal parts.
Does soil give a plant ready-made food? A. Yes B. No
Roots absorb water and minerals. Green parts use light energy to make food.
Roots take in water, and stems carry it through the plant.
structure
Water is scarce here. Find two features that help this cactus survive.
Match each feature to its job.
Which clue tells us this is a desert? A. No living things B. Hot every day C. Very little rainfall
Deserts receive very little rain. Some deserts are cold. Different desert plants have different root systems.
The thick stem stores water for dry times.
adaptation
Which model animals are harder to see? Make a prediction, then compare two backgrounds.
Record a prediction. Explore both backgrounds and collect the example results.
On pale ground, which group was harder to spot in this example trial? A. Dark models: 8 of 10 found B. Pale models: 3 of 10 found
Fewer pale models were found: 3 is less than 8. A different background can change which color blends in.
The pale models were harder to see on the pale ground.
camouflage
Look below the ground. Which parts may help the grass grow again?
Compare before and after grazing. Find the living growing parts.
When may this grass grow again? A. After every fire, whatever happens B. When its growing parts stay alive C. Only when its leaves are untouched
Living growing parts near the base can produce new growth. Damage can be too severe; recovery is not guaranteed.
The grass can grow again when its growing parts stay alive.
survive
Match each animal feature to the job it helps with. Use the evidence cards.
Connect the feature to the supported job.
Which evidence supports: this animal eats tough grass? A. Its coat is striped B. It is standing near a tree C. Flat teeth and observed grazing
Teeth and feeding observations support the claim. Coat color alone does not tell us what an animal eats.
Its flat teeth help it grind tough grass.
evidence
Keep the lamp in the same place. Change the canopy cover and compare the light below.
Predict, then compare sparse and thick canopy cover.
Which model canopy lets less light reach the floor? A. Thick canopy: 20 units B. Sparse canopy: 60 units
In this example model, 20 is less than 60. Only the canopy cover changes; the lamp stays fixed.
A thicker canopy lets less light reach the forest floor.
canopy
Compare the clues. Which feature or behavior helps in each situation?
Match the clue cards. Some strategies look very different.
Does a bright color prove that every animal is poisonous? A. Yes, always B. No, we need species-specific evidence
Some toxic animals have warning colors, but color alone is not proof. Hibernation is more than ordinary sleep.
Some animals blend in, but others have colors that warn predators.
predator
The ground is cold and the wind is strong. Find clues that help a low-growing plant.
Connect the plant features to the conditions shown.
Which feature matches the shallow growing layer shown? A. Shallow roots B. Very deep roots
Shallow roots fit the thin growing layer above frozen ground. This conclusion uses the conditions shown.
These plants grow close to the ground in the windy tundra.
tundra
Compare two model containers. Keep everything the same except the covering.
Check the fair-test conditions, then run the model.
Which container lost less heat in this model? A. Uncovered: 35 to 27 degrees B. Covered: 35 to 31 degrees
Covered water cooled by 4 degrees; uncovered water cooled by 8. The covering slowed heat loss. It did not create heat.
The covering slowed heat loss in this model.
heat loss
Compare camouflage as snow melts. Then follow food clues for a migrating bird.
Use the background and food evidence to match each response.
Do all animals migrate? A. No. Species have different responses. B. Yes. Every animal leaves in winter.
Some animals migrate. Others use different responses. Food availability is one important clue for this bird.
Some animals migrate to places where food is easier to find.
migrate
Build four displays. Match each environment with a feature and supporting evidence.
Complete four condition → feature → function chains.
An animal is white. Is that enough evidence to say it lives in the tundra? A. Yes. White animals always live there. B. We need more evidence.
Look for habitat, season, and behavior evidence. A single color does not identify a habitat.
This feature helps it survive because the thick stem stores water for dry times.
explain
Sort the water samples using their labels.
Sort the water samples using their labels.
Which sample is brackish? A. The mixed river-mouth sample. B. The low-salt river sample.
Brackish water has more salt than fresh water but less than seawater.
Water environments can have different amounts of salt.
Water Worlds
Move the sensor down and compare the light readings.
Move the sensor down and compare the light readings.
Where does this model show the most light? A. At the deepest point. B. Near the surface.
More light reaches the surface layer in this model.
In this model, less light reaches deeper water.
Follow the Light
Read each animal's needs before choosing a habitat.
Read each animal's needs before choosing a habitat.
Is matching the temperature alone enough? A. No, check the salt level too. B. Yes.
Both conditions must fit the needs on the card.
This habitat fits because its water conditions match the animal's needs.
Match the Habitat
Place the kelp where it can get light and stay attached.
Place the kelp where it can get light and stay attached.
Why does this kelp need a sunlit place? A. To hide from all water. B. To make food using light.
Kelp uses light to make food.
Kelp needs light to make its own food.
Stay in the Sunlit Zone
Follow the water past the fish's gills.
Follow the water past the fish's gills.
Which statement fits the fish? A. Its gills take oxygen from water. B. Its gills make new oxygen.
Gills take dissolved oxygen from water.
Fish use gills to get oxygen from water.
Breathing Below the Surface
Match each feature to the evidence of how it works.
Match each feature to the evidence of how it works.
Which action helps this jellyfish move? A. Growing roots into sand. B. Pushing water out.
Pushing water out helps move the jellyfish.
Different body parts help ocean animals move or stay safe.
Move and Stay Safe
Test the same model object in two water samples.
Test the same model object in two water samples.
What did we change? A. The salt in the water. B. The object's size and salt together.
Only salt level changed in this comparison.
In this test, the same object floats higher in saltier water.
Floating Fairly
Compare the plants and water in two wetlands.
Compare the plants and water in two wetlands.
Which clue best identifies the marsh in these pictures? A. Mostly large trees. B. Mostly grasses and other soft-stemmed plants.
The marsh shown is dominated by soft-stemmed plants.
Both places are wetlands, but their main plants are different.
Wetland Neighbors
Compare water moving through bare ground and a wetland model.
Compare water moving through bare ground and a wetland model.
Which model slows the flow in this trial? A. The planted wetland model. B. Both models must be identical.
The wetland model holds back some water and slows its flow.
Wetlands can hold water and slow its flow.
Slow the Flow
Observe what the model filter removes and what may remain.
Observe what the model filter removes and what may remain.
Can we drink the model's clearer water without checking it? A. Yes, clear means safe. B. No.
Clear water can still contain harmful substances or microbes.
A filter can remove some particles, but clear water is not always safe.
Clearer Is Not Always Safe
Find a place where the bird can reach food and rest.
Find a place where the bird can reach food and rest.
Why can this wetland help the bird? A. It offers food and resting places. B. Every wetland has no predators.
Food and resting places can support migrating birds.
This wetland provides food and a place to rest during migration.
A Feeding Stop
Build a reserve using the needs and evidence cards.
Build a reserve using the needs and evidence cards.
Is one water habitat suitable for every water animal? A. Yes. B. No, their needs differ.
Match each organism to its own needs and the available evidence.
This habitat works because it meets these needs.
Design a Water Reserve
Compare the soil before and after the worms move.
Compare the soil before and after the worms move.
Which statement is an observation? A. There are tunnels in the later picture. B. The worms want to build a city.
We can see the tunnels; we cannot observe the worms' wishes.
Worms can change the soil as they move through it.
Tiny Soil Engineers
Follow the stream before and after the dam is built.
Follow the stream before and after the dam is built.
What is one change shown upstream? A. All water disappears. B. More water collects.
The dam slows the stream and water collects upstream.
A beaver dam can change the water habitat.
The Beaver's Dam
Compare two lunches that provide the same amount of food.
Compare two lunches that provide the same amount of food.
Which change reduces single-use packaging in this example? A. A reusable lunch box. B. A larger disposable bag.
Reusing the box reduces the single-use packages counted here.
We can reduce waste by using a lunch box again.
Less Waste, Better Evidence
Put the before-and-after cards on a time line.
Put the before-and-after cards on a time line.
Which record shows a sudden change? A. A tree grew over ten years. B. Water rose within one hour.
The time labels show a rapid rise in water.
Some changes happen quickly, while others take a long time.
Fast and Slow Changes
Compare equal plants with different amounts of water.
Compare equal plants with different amounts of water.
What supports the claim that the middle amount worked best here? A. It had the most healthy leaves. B. Its pot was our favorite color.
Use the leaf records, not pot color, as evidence.
In this test, too much and too little water both harmed the seedlings.
Too Much or Too Little
Connect each living thing to what it needs.
Connect each living thing to what it needs.
If insects become scarce, what may happen to these insect-eating frogs? A. They will never need food again. B. Finding food may become harder.
Less available prey may make feeding harder.
Changes to one population can affect other living things.
A Web of Needs
Read the records before deciding what changed.
Read the records before deciding what changed.
Does every newly arrived species cause harm? A. No, we need evidence of its effects. B. Yes.
A new arrival is not automatically harmful.
We need evidence to explain how a new species affects a habitat.
A New Neighbor
Use the habitat cards to compare possible outcomes.
Use the habitat cards to compare possible outcomes.
Does seeing no birds in one pond prove the species is extinct? A. Yes. B. No.
Extinction means no living members of the species remain anywhere.
An animal may leave one place without its species becoming extinct.
Stay, Move, or Disappear?
Sort remains and traces that can become fossil evidence.
Sort remains and traces that can become fossil evidence.
Can a preserved footprint be a fossil? A. Yes. B. Only a whole animal can be a fossil.
Fossils can include preserved remains or traces of past life.
A fossil can preserve a body part or a trace of activity.
A Trace from the Past
Compare the teeth and choose a supported idea.
Compare the teeth and choose a supported idea.
What can a broad grinding surface suggest? A. The animal's exact skin color. B. It may help grind food.
Tooth shape supports a limited idea about feeding, not skin color.
This tooth is evidence about how the animal may have processed food.
Teeth Tell Part of a Story
Compare the mammoth and elephant evidence cards.
Compare the mammoth and elephant evidence cards.
Do similar fossils prove that no change occurred over time? A. No. B. Yes.
Some features can be similar while other features change.
These animals share some features, but they are not exactly the same.
Similar Is Not Identical
Choose a plan and explain which evidence supports it.
Choose a plan and explain which evidence supports it.
What should we do after trying a plan? A. Assume it always works. B. Measure the changes.
Check the results and revise the plan if needed.
Our plan may help, and we will collect data to check the results.
Restore with Evidence
Move the model lamp and mark the shadow.
Move the model lamp and mark the shadow.
Where is the shadow compared with the lamp? A. On the opposite side of the object. B. Always toward the lamp.
The object blocks light, leaving a shadow on the other side.
The shadow changes when the light's position changes.
A Moving Shadow
Keep the lamp still and turn the globe.
Keep the lamp still and turn the globe.
What causes day and night in this model? A. The Sun turning off. B. Earth's rotation.
Earth turns, so a place moves into and out of sunlight.
Earth rotates, causing day and night.
Turn Earth
Follow the marker through one full turn.
Follow the marker through one full turn.
About how long is a day? A. 24 hours. B. 24 months.
A day is about 24 hours.
One daily cycle takes about twenty-four hours.
One Turn, One Day
Compare the times, temperatures, and shadows in the table.
Compare the times, temperatures, and shadows in the table.
Does the shortest shadow occur at the highest temperature in this record? A. Yes. B. No.
The shortest shadow is at 12:00; the highest temperature is at 15:00.
The table shows different patterns for shadow length and temperature.
Read the Day's Record
Move Earth around the Sun while keeping its axis pointed the same way.
Move Earth around the Sun while keeping its axis pointed the same way.
What is the main cause of Earth's seasons? A. Its tilted axis as it orbits the Sun. B. The Sun turning cold every winter.
The tilt changes sunlight angle and daylight through the year.
Earth's tilt changes how sunlight reaches each hemisphere.
Tilt, Do Not Chase
Compare daylight records from the same town.
Compare daylight records from the same town.
Which example has more daylight? A. The winter day. B. The summer day.
Fourteen hours is longer than eight hours.
This town has more daylight in summer than in winter.
A Longer Day
Compare north and south at the same moment.
Compare north and south at the same moment.
If it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere, what season is it in the Southern Hemisphere? A. Winter. B. Always summer too.
The hemispheres have opposite seasons.
The two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time.
Two Hemispheres
Put the observation cards in order.
Put the observation cards in order.
What changes in these observations? A. The Moon becomes a different-shaped rock. B. How much of the lit side we see.
The Moon stays roughly round while its appearance changes.
The Moon looks different because we see different parts of its lit half.
A Moon Journal
Move the Moon around Earth and compare two views.
Move the Moon around Earth and compare two views.
During ordinary phases, how much of the Moon is lit by the Sun? A. About half. B. It grows from no rock to a whole rock.
Usually half is sunlit; our view of that half changes.
Sunlight lights half the Moon, while our view changes.
Light One Half
Compare an ordinary phase with a lunar eclipse.
Compare an ordinary phase with a lunar eclipse.
What happens in a lunar eclipse? A. Earth's shadow causes every crescent Moon. B. The Moon enters Earth's shadow.
A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow.
A lunar eclipse is different from an ordinary Moon phase.
Eclipse or Phase?
Use the pattern to predict the next observation.
Use the pattern to predict the next observation.
If the visible bright part has been growing, which is a reasonable next step? A. A larger bright part. B. A random unrelated shape.
A pattern supports a prediction, which observations can check.
I predict a larger bright part from this pattern.
Predict, Then Check
Choose a model and evidence for each sky pattern.
Choose a model and evidence for each sky pattern.
Which match is correct? A. Seasons—the Moon changing shape. B. Day and night—Earth's rotation.
Different sky patterns have different causes.
My model explains this pattern, and the records support it.
Explain the Sky
Sort the Sun, Earth, and Moon by their roles.
Sort the Sun, Earth, and Moon by their roles.
Which object makes its own light like other stars? A. The Sun. B. The Moon.
The Sun is a star; the Moon reflects sunlight.
The Sun is a star, and Earth is a planet that orbits it.
Our Star and Its Neighbors
Put the eight planets in order from the Sun.
Put the eight planets in order from the Sun.
Which planet comes after Earth and before Jupiter? A. Neptune. B. Mars.
Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.
Earth is the third planet from the Sun, followed by Mars.
Eight Planet Stops
Use the fact cards, not just the pictures, to group planets.
Use the fact cards, not just the pictures, to group planets.
Which evidence supports Earth's group? A. It has a rocky surface. B. It has a decorative blue border.
Use the stated physical properties.
The inner planets have rocky surfaces we can compare.
Read a Planet Card
Compare the orbit records for two planets.
Compare the orbit records for two planets.
What does an orbit describe? A. A planet's color. B. A path around another object.
An orbit is the path an object follows around another.
A planet rotates while it also orbits the Sun.
Paths Around the Sun
Match each description to the correct space object or event.
Match each description to the correct space object or event.
What is a meteor? A. The streak of light made as material enters the atmosphere. B. Every rock on the ground.
A meteor is the light phenomenon; a surviving piece on the ground is a meteorite.
A small space rock can produce a meteor when it enters the atmosphere.
Small Objects, Clear Names
Compare a distant target with and without a telescope model.
Compare a distant target with and without a telescope model.
What changed? A. The Moon moved next to Earth. B. The detail we can observe.
A telescope improves what we can observe; it does not move the object closer.
A telescope helps us see more detail in distant objects.
More Detail
Follow light through a simple telescope model.
Follow light through a simple telescope model.
Which part helps gather and focus light in this model? A. The lens. B. The decorative strap.
This telescope uses a lens; other telescopes can use mirrors.
This lens changes the path of light in the telescope.
Guide the Light
Compare two observation records before choosing a claim.
Compare two observation records before choosing a claim.
What can the repeated observations support? A. Every object in space orbits Earth. B. Some moons orbit Jupiter.
Repeated positions support the idea of moons orbiting Jupiter.
New observations can help us improve an explanation.
Evidence Can Change Ideas
Compare the same star field against dark and bright skies.
Compare the same star field against dark and bright skies.
Why are most other stars hard to see by day? A. The bright sky hides their faint light. B. They stop existing.
The stars remain, but the bright daytime sky makes them hard to see.
Most other stars are hard to see in the bright daytime sky.
Stars in the Daytime
Connect a given star pattern, then remove the guide lines.
Connect a given star pattern, then remove the guide lines.
Are the connecting lines real objects in space? A. Yes. B. No, they help us recognize a pattern.
The lines are guides drawn by people.
We use patterns to help identify parts of the night sky.
Patterns, Not Strings
Move Earth and compare which direction its night side faces.
Move Earth and compare which direction its night side faces.
Why can some night-sky patterns change with the season? A. Earth's night side faces different directions during its orbit. B. All stars go around Earth each year.
Earth's changing position changes our nighttime view.
As Earth orbits the Sun, our nighttime view changes.
A Different Night View
Build a report using a tool, a record, and a supported claim.
Build a report using a tool, a record, and a supported claim.
Can apparent brightness alone tell us a star's distance? A. Yes. B. No, more information is needed.
Brightness also depends on the star itself, not only distance.
Our observations support this idea, but we need more data for that question.
An Observatory Report
Measure the objects and record their properties.
Measure the objects and record their properties.
Which is a measurement? A. The block is 6 cm long. B. The block looks lovely.
A measurement gives a quantity and a unit.
We can describe matter using properties we observe or measure.
Describe Before You Guess
Move the solid, liquid, and gas into new containers.
Move the solid, liquid, and gas into new containers.
Which sample spreads to fill its closed container? A. The solid block. B. The gas.
A gas spreads through the space available to it.
Solids, liquids, and gases behave differently in containers.
Three States
Change the temperature and follow water's state.
Change the temperature and follow water's state.
What is condensation? A. Water vapor becomes liquid water. B. Ice becomes liquid water.
Condensation changes gas to liquid.
Cooling water vapor can make it condense into liquid water.
Heat and Cool
Weigh the closed container before and after the ice melts.
Weigh the closed container before and after the ice melts.
What happens to the total mass in this closed model? A. It becomes zero. B. It stays the same.
No material leaves or enters, so the total mass stays the same.
The state changes, but the total mass stays the same in this closed system.
Where Did the Mass Go?
Choose a rule and use it for every sample.
Choose a rule and use it for every sample.
Does every metal in these records stick to the magnet? A. No, aluminum does not in this test. B. Yes.
Different classification rules give different groups.
I grouped the samples by the property shown in the records.
Sort by Evidence
Use the model pieces to represent atoms of two elements.
Use the model pieces to represent atoms of two elements.
What does one labeled circle represent here? A. A real atom photographed at this size. B. An atom model.
The circles are models for particles too small to see unaided.
Matter is made of tiny particles we can represent with models.
Tiny Building Blocks
Find an element using its name and symbol.
Find an element using its name and symbol.
Which symbol matches oxygen? A. O. B. Fe.
O is the symbol for oxygen; Fe represents iron. O
The periodic table organizes elements and their symbols.
A Useful Element Map
Compare model mixtures with a model of water.
Compare model mixtures with a model of water.
Is a mixture of beans a new kind of bean? A. Yes. B. No, both kinds remain.
The parts of this mixture remain identifiable.
In this mixture, the different materials remain present.
Mix or Join?
Fold, cut, or melt the model material and compare what remains.
Fold, cut, or melt the model material and compare what remains.
Which is a physical change here? A. Cutting paper. B. Iron becoming rust.
Cut paper is still paper; cutting changes its shape and size.
A physical change does not by itself make a new substance.
Change the Shape
Compare the material before and after the recorded change.
Compare the material before and after the recorded change.
Does seeing bubbles always prove a chemical change? A. Yes. B. No, boiling water also has bubbles.
Bubbles are a clue; identify what substances are present.
A chemical change produces new substances.
Evidence of Something New
Compare the chalk in water with the chalk in vinegar.
Compare the chalk in water with the chalk in vinegar.
Which comparison helps separate crushing from reacting? A. Compare the original material and products. B. Compare only which cup is prettier.
Crushing changes size; reacting can form new substances.
We compare the evidence before deciding what kind of change occurred.
The Chalk Case
Build a report from measurements, particle models, and change records.
Build a report from measurements, particle models, and change records.
Is one color change enough to identify every chemical reaction? A. Yes. B. No.
Use several observations and information about the substances.
The evidence shows a change, but we need more information to explain it fully.
A Material's Story
Watch what changes when energy is transferred.
Watch what changes when energy is transferred.
Which is evidence of a change? A. The car starts moving. B. The car has a cheerful face.
Movement is an observable change in this example.
Energy transfers can cause changes.
Find the Change
Match each example to the energy form shown.
Match each example to the energy form shown.
Can a working lamp give off both light and heat? A. No, only one form is allowed. B. Yes.
A device can transfer energy in more than one way.
One device can change energy in several ways.
Energy in Everyday Life
Connect sunlight, a plant, and a plant-eating animal.
Connect sunlight, a plant, and a plant-eating animal.
Does the animal get food energy directly by standing in sunlight? A. No, it gets food energy by eating. B. Yes.
The animal gets chemical energy from food.
Sunlight helps plants make food, and animals obtain energy from food.
Follow Sunlight
Predict a change, run the model, and compare the result.
Predict a change, run the model, and compare the result.
Why does the model balloon expand when warmed? A. New air appears from nothing. B. The gas takes more space under these conditions.
Heating can make a flexible gas-filled container expand.
Heating the air can make it expand in this flexible model.
Warm Air, Moving Water
Compare the same car at two starting heights.
Compare the same car at two starting heights.
Before release, which has more gravitational potential energy relative to the same floor? A. The higher car. B. They must have none.
For the same car, a higher starting position means more gravitational potential energy.
The higher car has more stored energy relative to the same floor.
High and Low
Change only the release height and repeat each trial.
Change only the release height and repeat each trial.
What supports the conclusion for this setup? A. One car had a different color. B. All three higher-release trials went farther.
Repeated trials show the same direction of change here.
In this setup, a higher release point led to a longer travel distance.
Test the Ramp
Arrange the energy changes in the flashlight.
Arrange the energy changes in the flashlight.
Where was energy stored before the flashlight was switched on? A. In the battery's chemicals. B. In the painted arrow.
The battery stores chemical energy.
The battery's chemical energy is changed into electrical energy, then light and heat.
A Flashlight's Energy Story
Follow the energy after the moving toy slows down.
Follow the energy after the moving toy slows down.
Does all the energy simply vanish when the toy stops? A. Yes. B. No, energy is transferred to the surroundings.
Energy can spread to the surroundings, including as thermal energy.
Energy changes form and moves to the surroundings as the toy slows down.
Where Energy Goes
Watch the floating marker while a wave travels across the model.
Watch the floating marker while a wave travels across the model.
Does the marker travel all the way with the wave in this model? A. No, it moves around its starting place. B. Yes, always.
The disturbance travels while the marker moves locally.
A wave can transfer energy without carrying each marker all the way along.
A Wave Passes
Follow vibrations from the source through a material.
Follow vibrations from the source through a material.
Can ordinary sound travel through empty space with no matter? A. Yes, just like light. B. No.
Sound needs a material medium; light can travel through a vacuum.
Vibrations transfer sound energy through a material.
Sound Needs a Path
Connect a source to an output through a working path.
Connect a source to an output through a working path.
Which path can power the model lamp? A. Generator—connected wires—lamp. B. Generator—broken path—lamp always on.
A working connection is needed in this model.
Energy can move from one place to another.
Energy Travels
Choose energy paths that meet the station's needs.
Choose energy paths that meet the station's needs.
What is missing from a solar-only plan for a dark night? A. A brighter painted Sun. B. Stored energy or another source.
The plan needs a way to supply energy when sunlight is unavailable.
Our station needs an energy source, a transfer path, and a useful output.
Power the Research Station
Line up the holes so light can reach the screen.
Line up the holes so light can reach the screen.
Why does moving one card block the beam? A. The straight path is blocked. B. The lamp forgets to shine.
In this uniform-air model, light travels along a straight path.
The beam reaches the screen when the holes line up.
Find a Clear Path
Turn the mirror to guide light to the target.
Turn the mirror to guide light to the target.
What changed the light's direction? A. A command from the target. B. Reflection from the mirror.
Light changes direction when it reflects from the mirror.
A mirror reflects light in a direction we can predict.
Bounce the Beam
Compare reflections from smooth and rough surfaces.
Compare reflections from smooth and rough surfaces.
Why is the image less clear on the rough surface? A. Reflected light goes in many directions. B. Rough surfaces reflect no light at all.
Rough surfaces still reflect light, but the directions vary.
A rough surface scatters reflected light in different directions.
Clear or Scattered
Arrange the path from the lamp to the object and then the eye.
Arrange the path from the lamp to the object and then the eye.
How do we see the non-glowing toy? A. Our eyes send out searchlight beams. B. Light reflects from it into our eyes.
Reflected light enters the eyes and signals are sent to the brain.
We see the toy when light from it enters our eyes.
Light Reaches the Eye
Compare the eye model in brighter and dimmer surroundings.
Compare the eye model in brighter and dimmer surroundings.
What usually happens to the pupil in brighter light? A. It becomes smaller. B. It always fills the whole eye.
The iris adjusts the pupil opening to control incoming light.
The iris changes the size of the pupil to control incoming light.
The Pupil Window
Send white light through the prism model and compare the output.
Send white light through the prism model and compare the output.
Does a prism create all those colors from nothing? A. Yes, it paints the beam. B. No, it separates colors in the light.
A prism separates white light into a spectrum of colors.
White light contains many colors that a prism can separate.
Many Colors in White Light
Compare the light arriving at and leaving the red model object.
Compare the light arriving at and leaving the red model object.
In the white-light model, why does the object look red? A. More red light reaches the eye from it. B. It creates all red light itself.
The object reflects some colors more than others.
The color we see depends on the light that reaches our eyes.
Why Red Looks Red
Compare adding colored lights with passing light through a filter.
Compare adding colored lights with passing light through a filter.
Does mixing red and green light work like mixing red and green paint? A. Always exactly the same. B. Not necessarily; these are different processes.
Adding light differs from mixing pigments or filtering light.
Colored lights can add together, while filters remove some parts of the light.
Mix Lights, Test Filters
Test three materials in front of the same patterned card.
Test three materials in front of the same patterned card.
Can clear colored glass still be transparent? A. Yes, if objects can be seen clearly through it. B. No, color always means translucent.
Transparency depends on clear transmission, not simply the absence of color.
Some materials transmit light clearly, some scatter it, and others block it.
See Through or Not?
